summary: A two-part guide: the first for regular people who want to set up their own Directory User Interfaces to access the Directory, and the second for ISODE maintainers who want to build portable DUAs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instructions for setting up a program that looks things up in an electronic phone book, with one set for users and one for the people who build it.

questions: how to set up directory user agent
subtitle: How to set up programs that access the X.500 directory

tldr.problem: The X.500 directory system needed practical user-facing interfaces, and those interfaces required installation and configuration instructions that worked across different platforms.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides step-by-step instructions for both regular users setting up Directory User Agents and for system maintainers who want to package portable DUA implementations, covering four different DUA tools.
tldr.outcome: It enabled people to access X.500 using familiar tools like WHOIS or custom interfaces, though it is informational and documents specific historical implementations.

today: RFC 1373 is an Informational document describing historical X.500 DUA implementations. X.500 itself was eventually superseded by LDAP, which became the dominant directory protocol. The specific tools and instructions in this RFC are archival, though the concepts of directory access and user-friendly naming remain relevant in modern directory systems.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
RFC 1373 is a practical guide in two parts. The first helps regular users install and run Directory User Agents (DUAs)—programs that let you search the X.500 directory. The second helps system maintainers prepare these DUAs as portable packages for distribution.

The document covers four different DUA implementations: WHOIS, de, dixie/ud, and doog. Each one offers a different way to access the directory, from a simple command-line tool to a full interactive interface. The instructions assume you are running ISODE 8.0, the standard X.500 implementation software at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a how-to manual. It has two sets of instructions: one for people who want to use a directory lookup tool, and one for people who want to package it up for others to use.

sections.title: User Installation for Four DUAs
sections.content:
WHOIS is the simplest option. It uses a command-line interface to query a remote X.500 server. Users run whois -h hostname search-term where the search term follows UFN (User Friendly Naming) format: a comma-separated list of directory components like tignor,isi,ca,us.

De is a text-based interactive DUA. Installation requires creating configuration files, fetching a compressed archive, and running a compiler. Users may encounter a redeclaration error in general.h during compilation, which the RFC provides a workaround to fix.

Dixie/Ud is designed for users who search mostly within a single branch of the directory tree. It uses a preset base position (like an organization name), letting users search below that point without typing the full path. The dixie server must be running on the local ISODE machine.

Doog retrieves directory entries using UFN format. Like de, it requires downloading a tar archive, compilation, and configuration. Users interact with it at a command prompt.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tool has its own way of working. WHOIS is quick and simple. De and doog need you to compile and configure them. Ud is best if you mostly search in one department or organization.

sections.title: System Maintainer Packaging
sections.content:
Maintainers who run a DSA (Directory System Agent) can create portable packages of these DUAs for their users. The process differs for each tool.

For WHOIS, the maintainer configures the /etc/services and /etc/servers files (or /etc/inetd.conf on newer systems) to run a WHOIS emulation service. Users on machines without the DSA software can use a shell script that redirects them to the maintainer's WHOIS server.

For de and doog, the maintainer extracts the source from the ISODE distribution, configures files like detailor or the CONFIG.make variables, then compresses the result into a portable tar archive for distribution. These archives must include the required libraries and configuration files.

For dixie/ud, the maintainer downloads the latest dixie package, configures the Makefile variables to match the ISODE environment, and builds the server. The server then runs continuously to serve clients. Users download the dixie package separately and configure it to point to the maintainer's server.
sections.plainLanguage: If you run the directory server, you can package the lookup tools for others to use. Some need server changes, others just need you to distribute a package they can compile.

sections.title: Directory Concepts and UFN Format
sections.content:
The X.500 directory uses Distinguished Names (DNs) to identify entries. A DN is a path through the directory tree, written as components like @c=US@st=California@o=ISI. The @ symbol separates components, and the two-letter codes identify attribute types (c for country, st for state, o for organization).

User Friendly Naming (UFN) simplifies this. Instead of writing the full DN with attribute types, you write just the values as a comma-separated list: tignor,isi,ca,us instead of cn=Tom Tignor,ou=HPCC,o=ISI,st=California,c=US. DUAs that support UFN make the directory much easier for non-experts to use.

A Directory Information Tree (DIT) is the hierarchical structure of the directory, with the root at the top and organizations, departments, and people organized below. A DUA's base is a preset position in this tree where searches begin—usually an organization name.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is like a phone book, but organized in a tree. UFN format lets you write names the simple way: just list the parts separated by commas, like you would say a person's name.

references.text: Hardcastle-Kille, S., "User Friendly Naming", Work in Progress.
